transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/time: 2026-02-09 16:30 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Navarro (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Suncrest CTO), Maya Patel (Platform Lead), Samir Khan (Security), Olivia Park (SRE)

Auto-generated summary (brief, may be imperfect):
- Walkthrough of Redwood rate limiting primitives, org vs project key segmentation, fair-share routing, and burst controls.
- Discussed Suncrest requirements: multi-tenant isolation, SSO + audit logs, predictable billing for Q2 pilot.
- Agreed to POC scoping and exchange of traffic profiles, pricing, and security docs.

Topics:
- Key segmentation strategies
- Quotas and concurrency controls
- Burst and fair-share routing
- Dedicated capacity vs hosted fallback
- Security: KMS, audit logs, SSO

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. we're gonna run through a quick demo focused on segmentation and throttling — how teams usually map org and project keys and then the knobs you can use to protect tenant SLAs.
[00:10] Jordan: Yep thanks Alex, we'll be tight on time, but good to see you all. We're trying to figure out how to set limits per fund, per strategy, and also let internal experimentation teams burst without impacting client traffic.
[00:18] Priya: Great, thats exactly what we'll show — first the console, then the API snippets, then some Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Diego will hop in with the live console.
[00:27] Diego: (screen share noise) ok I'm in the console, top-left you can see the organizations list, Suncrest would be one org, inside it you can create projects, project keys are scoped to projects, org keys sit above and can be used by infra services.
[00:40] Maya: Quick question — is there a hard technical difference between using org key vs project key for rate limiting or is that just a UI construct?
[00:46] Priya: Good question. it's both a logical and policy boundary. org-level quotas are applied first — think of them as parent quotas — and project keys inherit but can have stricter per-project limits. Also routing policies can prefer project variants for low latency.
[00:59] [01:00] Samir: if we're running a PII-heavy model, we want those requests to stay on a private cluster. can we tie keys to private deployment?
[01:06] Priya: Yes — you can bind a project to a private deployment in the config. We have RBAC so only specific service principals can issue that project key. The bindings also show up in audit logs and you can integrate KMS for key rotation.
[01:20] Alex: I'll pause and show a sample policy JSON — (Alex types) so here's an example rolling-window quota, 100k tokens per day at org level, then per-project you can set concurrency caps and a burst token bucket.
[01:35] [01:40] Olivia: How deterministic is throttling? Our SRE needs predictable tail latencies — if a tenant bursts, will requests get queued or dropped?
[01:46] Diego: Two behaviors — you can configure queueing with a max wait (we default to fail-fast for public tiers), or set fair-share routing where excess is moved to lower-cost model variants.
[01:54] Priya: Also the Optimize tool can recommend batching windows so avg latency stays under your SLO while reducing token cost. it looks at actual sequence lengths and suggests per-model batch sizes.
[02:05] Jordan: For billing predictability, we need per-project metering exported to our billing system. do you support per-key export?
[02:11] Priya: Yep, usage is broken down by org/project key and tokens, with daily exports to S3 or direct webhook to your billing endpoint. The console shows token-level cost and top endpoints.
[02:20] Maya: Anything about sticky routing? We have high-value customers who must always hit the low-latency pool.
[02:25] Diego: You can set sticky routing rules based on project tags or IP ranges. That ensures certain keys always go to dedicated GPU pools. If that pool is full, fallback policies can either queue, failover to hosted, or spill to a compatible model variant.
[02:37] Samir: On compliance, we need SOC 2, customer-managed KMS, and proof of data residency. do you have these?
[02:43] Alex: Yes — we have SOC 2, KMS integrations, and private deployments in specific regions. We'll share the SOC2 and network architecture docs after this call.
[02:50] [03:00] Jordan: Ok let's dig into a real example — we run 3 production funds (fund-a, fund-b, sandbox). fund-a is highest priority, fund-b medium, sandbox gets best-effort. we want to allow sandbox to burst but never starve fund-a.
[03:12] Priya: Perfect. The way we'd implement is: org-level guarantee with reserved capacity for fund-a projects, then project-level burst buckets for sandbox with a lower priority. For real-time fairness you can use the fair-share queueing and set weights — e.g., fund-a weight 70, fund-b 20, sandbox 10.
[03:27] Diego: (typing) here's the routing tab — see policy editor. you can create a route rule: if project.tag=="fund-a" -> route to pool:dedicated-us-west priority high; else route to pool:shared. Also you can attach a concurrency limit per route.
[03:39] Maya: if sandbox spikes and uses all shared capacity, will it kick sandbox requests or throttle higher priority ones?
[03:44] Priya: With weighted fair-share it will throttle lower-weight tenants first; higher-weight tenants will keep throughput. you can also set 'protective reservations' so fund-a always has X qps reserved.
[03:53] Jordan: What about testing policies before they go live? We need a canary rollout for policy changes.
[03:58] Diego: We have a canary flag on routing policies. You can run a percent rollout (5-50-100) and check metrics via the console before full roll.
[04:07] [04:20] Olivia: I'm curious about policing at the API gateway level versus at the runtime. does Redwood enforce at edge so we don't hit runtime?
[04:26] Priya: Enforcement happens at the request broker — which is close to the edge, so most checks happen pre-queue. That means we avoid unnecessary runtime load. The broker also emits events to Kafka/observability for audit and alerting.
[04:37] Samir: Are there hooks for our existing rate-limiting proxies? We run Envoy with service mesh.
[04:41] Alex: You can integrate via the API — Redwood exposes pre-check endpoints or a token introspection API so your proxy can short-circuit. We have docs and an example Envoy filter.
[04:49] Maya: About concurrent requests — some of our models are long-running. If a request holds a worker for 30s, how do you count concurrency vs tokens?
[04:55] Priya: Concurrency is tracked per connection/worker; token consumption is separate. You can set both a concurrency cap and a tokens per minute cap. For long-running jobs you might want a queue with longer timeouts or run them on a separate pool with dedicated capacity.
[05:08] Jordan: Let's talk pricing tradeoffs — reserved pools vs hosted. If we reserve capacity for fund-a, what's the delta?
[05:14] Alex: Reserved pools come with a commit discount; they're billed monthly with usage included in the commit, and overage charged at a lower unit rate. Hosted is more elastic but has higher per-token unit cost. We'll send a tailored pricing sheet.
[05:24] [05:30] Diego: Show of console - Optimize suggests for your traffic a quantized 8-bit model for lower-priority workloads which reduces cost 40% with minimal quality drop on short prompts. You can auto-assign that model to sandbox projects.
[05:42] Maya: Any risk to quality when automatically routing to quantized variants? We run some replay-based QA.
[05:47] Priya: Optimize includes a small eval harness — you can pin prompt sets and compare outputs, we flag regressions. For critical traffic you can opt out of auto-routing.
[05:56] Jordan: How do we handle shared keys? Some internal tools use the master org key — is there risk on attribution?
[06:02] Diego: We recommend per-service project keys. Master org keys are powerful and we log all org-key usage, but attribution is coarser. For billing you'll want project keys.
[06:11] Samir: We need SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning and RBAC.
[06:15] Alex: Supported — we have SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, role-based roles, and you can restrict key creation to specific groups.
[06:22] [06:30] Jordan: Ok this is helpful. can you show an example of a quota rule in the UI and the equivalent API call?
[06:35] Diego: Sure — (types) in the UI you add a quota: type rolling-window, window 24h, limit 100000 tokens. API example: POST /v1/orgs/{org_id}/quotas with body -> (he reads fields; transcription glitch) "limit_tokens":100000 "window_seconds":86400.
[06:50] Maya: Small nit — we need near-real-time alerts when quotas hit 80%. how frequent are exports?
[06:56] Priya: Alerts can be wired to PagerDuty; usage metrics stream every minute for high-frequency metrics, and daily exports for billing. You can also subscribe to webhook notifications at threshold crossings.
[07:08] [07:15] Jordan: For the POC, timeline is aggressive — we'd like to run a 6-week pilot starting early March. The pilot scope: fund-a production traffic mirrored to Redwood, fund-b sampling, sandbox full traffic. success metrics: <150ms p95 for fund-a and no errors for 99.9% of fund-a requests.
[07:32] Priya: Sounds good. We'll propose a POC plan that includes traffic mirroring, baseline benchmarking, and a policy runbook.
[07:40] Alex: Next steps recap — we'll send pricing, SOC2 + network doc link, and a sample policy JSON. Priya will draft POC scope. Maya will share traffic profiles.
[07:50] Samir: one more question — what about tenant-level data retention? we need to ensure logs older than 90 days are purged and that we can delete customer data on request.
[07:56] Diego: We support retention policies and can configure automatic deletions. For private deployments you can have full control; for hosted we provide deletion APIs and retention settings.
[08:06] [08:15] Jordan: Great, thanks everyone. we'll sync after you share the docs.
[08:20] Alex: Thanks all, closing the demo.
